paper_title: Envisioning Agentic Robotics: A New Era of Robotic Systems

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The release of GPT-6 Astra marks the emergence of a new paradigm in robotics: agentic robotics. Within weeks, frontier models with agentic harnesses matched or exceeded task-specific policies on many embodied benchmarks. Instead of training a dedicated policy for each family of tasks, an agentic robotic system applies a foundation model to open-world embodied tasks. It operates in a closed loop: observing the environment, interpreting user intent, reasoning about the task, invoking skills and tools, verifying outcomes, and adapting its strategy. Despite these advances, the community has yet to converge on a shared definition, a reliable evaluation framework, or a research roadmap. We argue that Embodied System 2, realized by a foundation model together with an embodied harness, forms the decision-making core of agentic robotics. Its central challenge is to translate general-purpose reasoning into effective and verifiable actions under physical constraints such as limited reaction time, mechanical limits, unpredictable environment changes, and irreversible consequences. Motivated by this perspective, we propose an evaluation framework that measures both model capabilities and closed-loop system performance. Furthermore, we identify the principles that carry over from digital to physical agents and the challenges that must be addressed to achieve reliable physical autonomy. On top of the Embodied System 2 and the evaluation framework, we envision a research roadmap toward sustained autonomy: the ability to perform work safely and reliably with progressively broader responsibility, from executing individual primitives to fulfilling standing roles.

Introduction central goal of robotics is to enable robots to translate human intent into desired outcomes in the physical world. Early autonomous robots often integrated hand-engineered components for perception, planning, and control within modular or layered architectures (Nilsson, 1984; Gat et al., 1998). Since then, advances in deep learning have allowed robots to learn increasingly complex behaviors. Policies learned in simulation, mostly with deep reinforcement learning, have produced agile locomotion (Hwangbo et al., 2019) and versatile humanoid whole-body control by tracking human motion data (Liao et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2026c; Liao et al., 2026). However, these simulation-trained policies remain specialized to specific tasks and embodiments, limiting their ability to generalize across diverse and open-ended environments. To move beyond task-specific controllers and enable robots to follow human instructions, the field has increasingly turned toward models that unify perception, language understanding, and action generation within single framework. Among them, visionlanguage-action (VLA) models, exemplified by the 𝜋 series, combine vision-language pretraining with diverse robot data to learn general policies that map visual observations and language instructions to actions (Black et al., 2025a,b). More recently, world-action models (WAM) integrate video-based modeling of physical dynamics with robot policy learning (Ye et al., 2026a; Yuan et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026c). Together, these advances have broadened robot capabilities. Yet reliable generalization remains central challenge, as policy performance can still deteriorate when scenes or instructions change (Zhou et al., 2025c). To address this generalization challenge, major line of research focuses on scaling and diversifying training data for VLA and WAM policies (Zheng et al., 2026; Dyna Robotics, 2026a). These efforts draw on diverse data sources, including real-robot data (Black et al., 2025a), UMI demonstrations (Chi et al., 2024), egocentric human data (Zheng et al., 2026), and multimodal web data (Brohan et al., 2023). The release of GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026a,b) and its early applications to robotics offered different perspective on this challenge. In an early evaluation, the model outperformed trained policies on many robotic benchmarks without task-specific fine-tuning (Zhang et al., 2026c). Subsequent work explored its use with learned policies and robotic tools (Galbot Team et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026b). These results suggest that generalization can also be achieved by relying on general-purpose models knowledge and reasoning to organize and adapt behavior during execution. This perspective motivates paradigm shift from policy-centric robotics to agentic robotics, by shifting the focus from learned action policies (Figure 2a) to an agent that pursues goals by coordinating skills and tools, evaluating outcomes, and adapting its decisions (Figure 2b). Despite this progress, the community still lacks shared understanding of agentic robotics or reliable evaluation framework. The scope of the paradigm, its relationship to existing forms of robot autonomy, and the organization of its constituent functions remain insufficiently clarified (Qin et al., 2026a). Furthermore, differences in experimental conditions and system configurations also make it difficult to compare results across studies. For example, RoboDojo evaluations of Astra vary in the task-knowledge sources they use and the action budgets they permit (Zhang et al., 2026c; SenseNova et al., 2026); separately, Harness VLA shows substantial performance gains from execution memory when the planner and VLA are held fixed (Zhang et al., 2026f). All of these results underscore the need to establish what constitutes the agentic system, which capabilities are being assessed, and under what conditions comparisons are meaningful. These conceptual and methodological challenges call for unified framework that clarifies the agentic workflow by specifying the functional roles of its components and how they interact. Such framework can provide shared conceptual foundation for characterizing agentic robotics, developing valid and comparable evaluations at the model and system levels, and formulating research roadmap. The roadmap connects this progression to four research directions, including continual improvement from physical experience. Finally, we conclude with several guidelines to verify and evaluate the progress of agentic robotics. 2. Overview of Agentic Robotics We adopt system-level view of agentic robotics: an agent interprets the users intent, decides how to proceed, orchestrates skills and tools at run time, and verifies their physical effects against the intended goal. Feedback from verification guides subsequent decisions, enabling the system to adapt its actions, recover from failures, and seek clarification or assistance when needed. We first present reference architecture that defines the responsibilities and interfaces of S2, S1, and S0. We then go through the agentic loop and examine three system-level properties: operation across multiple timescales, responsiveness during deliberation, and state persistence across tasks. 2.1. Reference Architecture In general, an agentic robot requires three functional roles: S2 interprets intent, reasons about goals and constraints, orchestrates capabilities, and verifies outcomes; S1 provides skills and callable modules; and S0 provides the body interface and local real-time control. Note that this decomposition is functional: one model may serve several roles, and one role may span several models or modules. Figure 3 shows the three systems and their interfaces, together with the user, the robot body, the physical world, and real-time event monitor. The systems typically run on different timescales, but timing alone does not distinguish them. We describe them from S2 downward, focusing on their responsibilities and interactions. System 2: Intent, Reasoning, Orchestration, and Verification. S2 is the functional layer that interprets intent, reasons about goals and constraints to make decisions, orchestrates skills and tools accordingly, and verifies outcomes to adapt subsequent decisions toward the intended goals. It decides whether to act, gather information, ask for clarification, continue, retry, replan, or stop. When acting, it chooses capability and specifies the call, which may invoke an S1 skill or tool, or send an action target directly to S0. It checks the returned evidence against the intended goal before deciding on the next subtask. In hierarchical systems such as Hi Robot (Shi et al., 2025) and Gemini Robotics (Gemini Robotics Team, 2025a,b, 2026b), high-level vision-language model contributes to the orchestration: it interprets instructions and feedback before delegating the next subtask to an action model. In our framework, S2 is realized by foundation model and an embodied harness. The S2 foundation model supplies knowledge, understanding, and reasoning, and proposes the next decision from the context it receives. The embodied harness supplies the runtime that assembles the models context and turns its decisions into constrained, observable, and verifiable execution. Concretely, it has five core parts. context manager assembles current observations, task progress, interaction history, and the state of the world, the user, and the body. tool interface exposes S1 skills, permitted S0 calls, code execution, and other tools to S2. planner maintains and revises task plans given the foundation models proposals or dedicated planning routines. memory stores, retrieves, updates, and removes information beyond the current context. verifier judges from evidence whether step achieved its subgoal and whether the task is complete. Existing systems implement some of these parts: Inner Monologue (Huang et al., 2023b) feeds scene and skill-success signals back into planning; SCOPER (Wei et al., 2026a) updates an evidence memory and verifies progress to guide recovery. S1 provides skills and callable modules that perform the functions S2 delegates, including action execution, perception, and motion planning. Specifically, action execution modules map observations to actions within the scope of subtask, such as VLA policies (Black et al., 2025b,a; NVIDIA et al., 2025c), world-action models (WAMs) (Dyna Robotics, 2026b), locomotion policies, and navigation policies. Perception modules extract task-relevant estimates from sensor data through detection (Minderer et al., 2022), segmentation (Carion et al., 2025), pointing (Deitke et al., 2024), and pose estimation (Wen et al., 2024). Motion planning modules turn goal into feasible motion (Sundaralingam et al., 2023; Sundermeyer et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025). single call may combine several of these categories. For example, grasp call may segment the object, select grasp function, plan path, and execute it. Programs written by S2 likewise serve as S1 skills when they execute delegated behavior (Yang et al., 2026j). System 0: Body Interface and Local Real-Time Control. S0 is the embodiment-specific layer that executes control targets in real-time loop. Examples are whole-body tracking and balance for humanoid, gait tracking and stabilization for quadruped, inverse kinematics and trajectory tracking for an arm, and chassis control for mobile base. For humanoids, whole-body tracking is increasingly handled by general-purpose controllersoften called behavior foundation modelsthat are pretrained at scale (Yuan et al., 2025a), for example by learning to track large human-motion datasets (Luo et al., 2026c; Liao et al., 2026). S0 receives control targets from S1, or from S2 through permitted action interface, and reports state estimates such as joint positions, contact, and pose. It maintains stability and enforces the bodys control limits without waiting for S2 to deliberate. Real-Time Event Monitor. lightweight real-time event monitor runs alongside the three systems. At high rate, it watches the user, the robot body, and the physical world for events that cannot wait for S2 to decide. Such events include sudden command or interjection from the user, an unexpected body movement caused by collision or fault, and change in the scene such as person entering the workspace. In practice, the monitor may use small streaming vision-language model (VLM), rule-based detectors, or both. It interrupts S2 when an event may change the task. When an event demands an immediate reaction, it may apply its predefined safety rules and trigger protective response in S0, such as stopping or slowing the current motion. In general, commands flow downward and evidence flows upward across the three systems. In the downward direction, we divide the execution of decision into three typical paths by how S2 reaches the body, as shown in Figure 4. In layered orchestration, S2 invokes S1 skills and tools, which produce the actions that S0 executes. In direct control, S2 bypasses S1 and controls S0 through an action interface, as several systems built on frontier models do (Zhang et al., 2026c; Yang et al., 2026j). Direct control does not place the foundation model inside the real-time control loop: S0 still runs its own local loop, and the action interface defines what S2 may send to it. In code as policy, S2 writes code that plays the role of S1 at run time (Liang et al., 2023); the code may execute several actions before S2 decides again. Note that these paths are not alternative architectures: one system may use all three within single task. In the upward direction, S0 reports the state of the body. Each call should return the observations available at that point and an execution status, allowing S2 to assess the outcome. Outside this call chain, the event monitor signals S2 and S0 without being invoked. The three systems also differ in how directly they depend on the body. S0 must account for the robots dynamics and control interface, whereas S1 skills depend on the actions and observations that the body provides. Agentic Loop: From Intent to Verified Outcome Consider the request, Find the red cup and bring it to the dining table. Given this request, S2 interprets it and plans four subtasks: locate, grasp, carry, and place the cup. It first invokes perception, and the harness records the cups identity, location, and observation time. Then S2 invokes grasp skill and checks the returned observation to make sure that the cup is held securely for transport. During transport, S1 and S0 maintain control while new observations inform S2s subsequent decisions. After placement, S2 verifies that the cup is supported by the table at the requested location. Each stage forwards state to the next, and the harness distinguishes past event, the cup was grasped, from current state, the cup is still held. Suppose instead that the user interjects while the robot is grasping the red cup: Not the red cup, the blue one. The event monitor detects the interjection and interrupts S2. S2 recognizes that the revised goal conflicts with the current action and requests that the grasp be paused or canceled. cancellation request alone is insufficient: before dispatching conflicting action, the harness must confirm that execution has stopped and that the body is in suitable holding state. S2 then refreshes its observations and replans to retrieve the blue cup. Sometimes skill reports success even though the action did not succeed. In this case, verification also catches unreported failures. For example, the grasping skill reports success on the blue cup, but the wrist camera shows that the cup is still on the shelf: the grasp was executed as commanded but missed. S2 attributes the miss to grasp point that was occluded by the cups handle. It therefore observes the cup from another side and retries with different grasp rather than repeating the same call. The example above traces six logical steps, which form feedback cycle. Step 1: Interpret Intent. The user expresses intent, which may be explicit (put the mugs in the dishwasher) or implicit in preferences and context. S2 combines the request with the context assembled by the harness, such as known preference that determines where cup belongs. Across the whole system, three properties should hold. 10 Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems Multiple Timescales. The components typically operate on different timescales. S0 typically runs locally at roughly 50 Hz to 1 kHz (Luo et al., 2026c; Dyna Robotics, 2026b; Figure AI, 2026a). S1 control skills run continuously while subtask executes, at rates that depend on the platform and the task. Some commercial stacks report rates from about 5 Hz to 200 Hz (Dyna Robotics, 2026b; Figure AI, 2025b; NVIDIA et al., 2025c). By contrast, perception and motion planning modules are invoked on demand and return results after their computation finishes. S2 does not run at fixed rate: it could be invoked when skill finishes or fails, when new observations arrive, when the event monitor reports an event, or when the user speaks. frontier model in this role may take from several seconds to tens of seconds per decision (Xu et al., 2026d; Galbot Team et al., 2026), although this latency is an implementation property, not defining feature of S2. Continuous Responsiveness. While S2 is deliberating or skill is executing, the physical world or the body state may change, and the user may revise an instruction. The event monitor should watch for these changes and remain responsive throughout deliberation and execution. Current systems achieve this responsiveness in different ways. Gemini Robotics-ER 2 treats new prompt received during generation as an interruption of model reasoning and of pending tool calls (Google, 2026). MIRA combines streaming speech understanding with interruptible motion (Lin et al., 2026). ProAgent pairs fast model that decides whether and when to intervene with slower model that decides what to do (Yang et al., 2026g). In our architecture, the safety rules reside in the event monitor, so protective stop can be requested in time. Persistent State. The harness should keep persistent state. We call one task an episode and continuous period of use session, which may contain many episodes. Within an episode, the harness tracks progress, object identities, and previous attempts. Across episodes and sessions, it maintains what the robot has learned about the environment, the users preferences, and the body state. The record of the physical world must be reconstructed from observations and could become stale without notice, as when an object is moved. Persistent memory should therefore record when and how each item was obtained and allow revision, rather than treat stored observation as permanent fact. 3. Embodied System 2: Foundation of Agentic Robotics The previous section described how S2 interacts with S1 and S0. In this section, we examine S2 itself. We first define S2 and give criterion for identifying it in robotic system. We then examine how the foundation model and embodied harness contribute to its eight capabilities and how physical constraints shape its operation. 3.1. Definition We formally define Embodied System 2 as follows. Definition (Embodied System 2). Embodied System 2 (Embodied S2) is the functional layer of an agentic robot that interprets intent, reasons about goals and constraints to make decisions, orchestrates skills and tools accordingly, and verifies outcomes to adapt subsequent decisions toward the intended goals. In this paper, Embodied S2 refers specifically to an implementation in which foundation model and an embodied harness jointly fulfill that role. Hereafter, we use Embodied S2 and S2 interchangeably and reserve S2 foundation model for the model inside Embodied S2 alone. The above definition has three notable features. First, it is anchored in intent rather than in 11 Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems fixed task specification: the objective is world state that satisfies the user. Reaching it may require clarifying an ambiguous request, inferring an unstated preference, or accommodating change of mind. Second, it rests on responsibility: S2 makes high-level decisions, whereas S1 and S0 make action-level decisions within the scope that S2 delegates to them. Third, it includes the harness, because the state on which S2s decisions depend, namely that of the world, the user, and the body, is usually not supplied by the environment directly. This state must be assembled by the harness from partial, noisy, and aging observations. Identifying S2. Labels such as System 2, embodied brain, planner, and orchestrator are applied inconsistently, so we identify S2 by functionality, not by name. component, or set of components, acts as S2 if and only if it closes the loop of the definition, which requires two kinds of decision: (i) decisions on how to proceed: interpreting the intent and, given the goals and constraints, either choosing the next subgoal and the skill or tool that should achieve it, together with the arguments of the call, or choosing to continue, retry, replan, ask, or stop; and (ii) decisions on outcomes: judging from evidence whether the previous step, or the task as whole, achieved its goal, so that the next decision can adapt accordingly. Both kinds of decision must also be identifiable from outside: either the components output interface exposes them, or controlled replacement experiment reveals them. component that makes only one kind of decision implements part of S2 but does not act as S2 on its own. For example, planner that chooses and sequences skills without checking their effects orchestrates but never verifies. By contrast, success detector makes neither kind of decision: it scores an observation, but whether that score settles the outcome of step or of the task, and what follows from it, is decided elsewhere. State estimators in S0, perception modules in S1, world models, and the real-time event monitor likewise supply evidence without deciding what it means for the task: they inform S2 but do not act as S2. Because the criterion concerns function, it applies to any implementation, including classical planners and behavior trees. Borderline Cases. In dual-system VLAs whose upper module emits only latent representation, such as Helix (Figure AI, 2025b) and GR00T N1 (NVIDIA et al., 2025c), high-level decisions cannot be read from the interface. We therefore do not classify the upper module as S2 unless replacement experiments show otherwise. Conversely, model that first emits subtask and then the actions to achieve it, such as 𝜋0.5 (Black et al., 2025a), or G0.5 with its chain-of-thought stream enabled (Liu et al., 2026e), makes an identifiable decision on how to proceed. Its subtask stage therefore implements part of S2, even though it shares weights with S1. As the authors of Hi Robot note, the separation of roles at the model level is not fundamental to this design (Shi et al., 2025). Decision frequency is not part of the criterion. model trained for the S2 role may decide about once per second (Shi et al., 2025), whereas frontier model queried over network may take tens of seconds per decision (Galbot Team et al., 2026). Either acts as S2 if it makes both kinds of decision. Speed determines whether an S2 is useful in given setting, so we treat it as physical constraint rather than as part of the definition. Nor is the granularity of the outputs part of the criterion. component that emits end-effector targets or programs acts as S2 only if it also makes both kinds of decision, and an S2 that orchestrates skills remains S2 when it emits pose directly (Figure 4). Relation to Existing Definitions. Our definition builds on recent proposals that describe S2 as the embodied brain that selects skills and checks their effects (Luo et al., 2026b; Wei et al., 2026a), and on work that distinguishes model from the runtime around it (Liang et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2026e). Our definition differs from these works in two respects: it provides an explicit, testable criterion, and it counts the harness as part of Embodied S2. Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems 3.2. S2 Foundation Model The S2 foundation model turns the context assembled by the harness into decisions. It may be general frontier model used without embodied training, an embodied foundation model post-trained for embodied tasks, or the reasoning stage of larger model that also produces actions. In each case, it inherits broad knowledge and reasoning from large-scale pretraining. However, its role differs from that of chatbot or coding agent, since its decisions are carried out by body in the physical world. Doing the work that the definition assigns to S2 in the physical world requires eight abilities (Figure 6). Knowledge, understanding, and reasoning reside mainly in the foundation model; tool use, memory, cross-embodiment, safety, and efficiency arise from the foundation model and the embodied harness together. For each ability, we describe what it is, why S2 needs it, and how the foundation models share of it can be cultivated. Knowledge. Knowledge comprises the general facts, concepts, and procedures on which S2 draws. It matters because S2 must fill the gaps that request leaves open, such as where dish belongs or that heavy box goes below light one. World knowledge covers objects, everyday relations, and culture. Embodied knowledge covers materials, physical laws, tools and mechanisms, the preconditions and effects of actions, and the structure, sensing, and kinematics of robots. Programming knowledge covers languages, algorithms, and software interfaces, which empowers an S2 model to compose skills with code (Liang et al., 2023). Knowledge requires broad coverage, which only pretraining-scale data provides. World and programming knowledge are therefore inherited largely from pretraining on web text, images, and code. Embodied knowledge is sparser in these sources but needs the same breadth. It should therefore also be acquired during pretraining, by adding embodied data to the corpus at scale rather than leaving it to the smaller and narrower data of post-training. Suitable sources include egocentric and instructional videos that show how people handle objects and what their actions achieve, and robot trajectories paired with language, which tie actions to their preconditions and effects. For example, Magma includes human videos and robot data in its pretraining (Yang et al., 2025a). Others are technical documentation, such as robot specifications, kinematic models, and controller interfaces, and simulated data on physical properties and dynamics, such as mass, friction, stability, and deformation. Understanding. Understanding is S2s grasp of the current situation: the state of the world, what the user wants, the state of the robot, and what cannot be inferred from the available observations. Understanding of the robot extends beyond its body to the capabilities beneath S2: which S1 skills exist, what their preconditions and failure modes are, and which S0 interfaces, reference frames, and limits apply. It differs from embodied knowledge: knowing how inverse kinematics works is knowledge, whereas judging whether this robot, in its current state, can reach given pose is understanding. Understanding matters because every decision rests on it: an understanding error could propagate into planning and execution. Understanding of the robot lets S2 choose the level at which to act: whether to orchestrate skill, control S0 directly, ask, or decline. Understanding of progress and completion, in turn, makes verification possible. Reasoning. Reasoning is how S2 decides what to do next and revises that decision as evidence arrives. It encompasses inferring the intent behind an underspecified request, deciding when to ask for clarification, planning over long horizons, diagnosing failures, and handling interruptions. Reasoning is therefore central to S2s role. Two of these sub-abilities are particularly relevant to the execution paths in Figure 4: skill selection and orchestration, which decides which existing skills and tools to use and in what order (the layered-orchestration path), and executable action inference, which decides which action target to send directly when no suitable skill exists, without placing the model inside the real-time control loop (the direct-control path). Memory. Memory is the ability to retain what the current observation no longer shows, to use it in later decision, and to replace it when it becomes stale. robot must remember objects and their attributes, locations, the order of completed steps, procedures demonstrated earlier, world state revealed by interaction, and the preferences of the people it serves. Memory matters because physical work extends beyond what camera sees at any moment and acting on an outdated memory can cause failures (Liang et al., 2026a). The models role is to decide what is worth recording and whether memory still applies to the present situation; storing and retrieving information beyond the context window is the harnesss role. The model learns these judgments from tasks in which earlier observations must be recalled and revised as the world changes. Cross-Embodiment. Cross-embodiment is the ability to achieve given objective when the body changes in appearance, morphology, end effector, action space, or dynamics. The same goal may require different paths or motions on different platforms. For example, wheeled base may need 14 Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems longer route around obstacles that legged robot can cross. It matters because the value of general S2 lies in serving many bodies without being rebuilt for each. To serve new body, the model must understand it, adapt the plans and action parameters to it, and reuse experience gained on other bodies without letting that experience interfere. Safety. Safety is the ability to avoid harm along the entire action chain: recognizing risk, predicting its consequences, choosing cautious response, preventing harm before acting, monitoring during execution, recovering afterward, responding in time, and coordinating stop. Specifically, risk recognition identifies hazards in the scene and in the request, such as hot liquid near childs hand or knife handed over blade first. Consequence prediction anticipates what an action would do in this particular scene. For example, pulling one box from stack may topple the rest. prudent decision chooses whether to proceed, proceed more cautiously, gather information, ask, or refuse, within the robots validated capability limits, and prefers reversible or information-gathering actions under high uncertainty. Prevention before action checks planned call against these predictions before it is dispatched. During execution, S2 monitors whether the situation still matches its assumptions and replans when conditions changefor instance, when person enters the workspace. After failure, safe recovery first returns the robot and the scene to safe state and only then retries. stop decided by S2 must be coordinated with S1 and S0 so that the running skill halts in safe state. Safety is thus property of decisions in the action loop rather than of answers about hazards. The model does not carry this responsibility alone. Hard limits on force and speed, protective stops, and permissions are enforced by the harness, S1, and S0 below the model, so that safety never rests on the models judgment only. Efficiency. Efficiency is the ability to make good decision with low latency and with few tokens per decision. It matters because the physical world does not wait. decision that arrives after the situation has changed is useless or even dangerous, and every token adds both latency and cost, which accumulate over hours of operation. Its tool interface exposes every tool with schema, units, reference frames, and failure semantics, so that the models choices of tool and arguments refer to well-defined physical quantities. Recent systems point to four contracts (Wang et al., 2026c; Deng et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026c). An observation snapshot records when, where, and in which reference frame each observation was captured, and which calibration was in force. capability contract specifies skills inputs and units, preconditions, expected effects, resources, time limits, behavior on cancellation, and the state it leaves for the next skill. An invocation record links each call to its task, subgoal, Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems attempt, inputs, and final status, so that retries and late results can be traced. An evidence bundle records the observations, controller states, and verifier outputs on which judgment of success was based. Together, the contracts define minimal lifecycle for every physical call: propose admit dispatch execute confirm the terminal state verify the effect commit progress. The lifecycle has explicit branches for rejection, failure, cancellation, and unknown outcomes. The branch for unknown outcomes is necessary since timeout is not evidence that an action did not run. Before retrying, the harness should query the execution handle and observe the scene again; repeating command that has in fact completed can execute physical action twice. Cancellation passes through three distinct states as well: requested, accepted, and completed; the return of cancel call does not show that the robot has stopped. Two systems illustrate this discipline: RegenHarness separates models proposal from controllers termination and verified completion (Wang et al., 2026c), and DynaHarness records evidence under shared physical execution contract (Deng et al., 2026). Skill boundaries require the same care, because grasp can succeed in way that obstructs the subsequent insertion. Three Loops. harness supports three feedback loops. The sensorimotor loop determines how actions respond to physical state; it resides in S1 and S0. The planning loop determines how the next subgoal is chosen after each result; it is the main loop of S2. The evolution loop determines which capabilities the next run will use, such as skills, prompts, context rules, tools, or model weights revised from experience. frozen model can still improve through the evolution loop, and fixed program can still react through the sensorimotor loop. Conflating the three therefore obscures where reaction or an improvement originates. Because the harness consists of code and data, S2 can also modify it: several recent self-improving robot agents revise tools, skills, context rules, or recovery policies rather than model weights (Tian et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026c; Lee et al., 2026b). Many hard problems reside in the harness: multi-rate scheduling, cancellation that actually stops motion, consistent state across asynchronous components, and accountable records of what the robot did and why. Existing robotics infrastructure provides many building blocks for these problems, including action protocols with feedback and cancellation, middleware for real-time data flow (Macenski et al., 2022), and behavior trees with bounded recovery (Colledanchise and Ögren, 2018). Runtime governance layers add policy checks, capability admission, monitoring, rollback, and human override around the agent (Qin et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026d). The harness also carries the systems share of efficiency: it calls the model only when decision is needed, compiles stable sub-processes into programs that run without the model, and delegates fast loops to S1 and S0. What remains is to connect these mechanisms to model and to measure what each mechanism contributes. Existing measurements already show that the harness substantially influences overall performance. For example, interfaces that let the model check and retry locally outperformed plain tool calling while using fewer model calls (Si et al., 2026). Verification can be decisive: in one ablation, with the model fixed, removing HumanCLAWs verifier nearly eliminated navigation success (Siyao et al., 17 Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems 2026). Constraints Imposed by the Physical World Unlike digital environments, the physical world involves embodiment, continuous dynamics, and irreversible consequences (Section 5). Observations are partial and noisy, actions are delayed and constrained by actuator limits, and contact-rich interactions are governed by friction, compliance, and wear that are difficult to model exactly. Whatever model fills the S2 role, the physical world constrains how it may decide: decisions face deadlines, can be interrupted at any moment, must fit the robots compute and cost budgets, and rest on aging, partial observations. Answer accuracy captures none of these constraints, which the following paragraphs discuss in turn. Capped Scaling. For frontier models, capability has grown with the computation: more reasoning tokens generally yield better answers at the cost of longer latency (OpenAI, 2024). We call this regime monotonic scaling. robot cannot follow it since the physical world imposes deadlines. decision is useful primarily when it arrives before the situation that it addresses has changed, for instance before an object rolls off the table or grasp slips. Embodied S2 therefore requires different regime, which we call capped scaling: becoming more capable within fixed decision deadline (Figure 7). What matters is not how long the model deliberates but how well the system decides within the time available. Humans meet physical deadlines through layered control (Todorov, 2004): grip-force corrections begin about 74 ms after an object starts to slip (Johansson and Westling, 1987), and the reflex responses that support recovery from trip begin 60 to 140 ms after it (Eng et al., 1994). Deliberation handles only what cannot be handled faster. An S2 should likewise match its reasoning effort to the time available and delegate fast loops to S1 and S0. For the model, capped scaling means gaining capability within fixed budget of tokens and time rather than by generating more tokens. In terms of the S2 foundation model, capped scaling calls for concise reasoning. Much of the reasoning that people perform when acting physically is never verbalized, such as where to put heavy box when packing or how to approach fragile glass. Robots often operate with limited connectivity, and single task may involve hundreds of decisions. Therefore S2 must run within the robots compute and power budget or tolerate network latency and outages. The cost per task should be acceptable as well. While S2 deliberates, S1 and S0 keep acting and the world keeps changing, so the observation behind decision has aged by the time the decision takes effect. S2 must therefore reason about the age of its information, request fresh observations when necessary, and express decisions in forms that remain valid under small changes. For instance, it should issue place the cup on the shelf rather than fixed joint configuration. Partial observability compounds the problem: S2 must distinguish what it observes, what it infers, and what it does not know, and act on this uncertainty by looking again, asking, or abstaining. Within system-level evaluation, it also matters whether the harness is fixed across the models compared, supplied by each models developer, or itself the object of study, because harness changes alone can move success lot. Across these two levels, Figure 9 organizes the evaluation into nine dimensions with 53 subdimensions: the eight abilities of Embodied S2 (Figure 6) and cost, which is not an ability but measure of the resources the system consumes. The 29 embodiment-related sub-dimensions are specific to embodiment or depend strongly on it, and standard evaluations of general language models rarely cover them. The reasoning budget appears under efficiency rather than reasoning because it is variable to be controlled and reported, not an ability in itself. Fulfillment of user intent is not separate dimension but the end-to-end outcome that all dimensions serve. The dimensions play different roles and are not orthogonal. Knowledge, understanding, and reasoning describe what the foundation model can do. Tool use, memory, and cross-embodiment describe what the system achieves through its harness and across bodies. Safety constrains all of them. Efficiency describes how quickly and with how few tokens the system decides, and cost the resources it consumes. Results should therefore be reported as profile across dimensions rather than summed into single score. Knowledge. Knowledge tests probe the models facts, concepts, and procedures through self-contained, single-turn questions without tools. World knowledge spans objects and everyday relations, life science, matter, the Earth and the universe, and geography, history, and culture; CommonsenseQA (Talmor et al., 2019) is candidate source. Embodied knowledge spans materials and physical properties, basic physical laws, object functions, tools and mechanical mechanisms, action preconditions and effects, robot structure and actuation, sensing and feedback, and coordinate systems and kinematic fundamentals. PIQA, NEWTON, and RoboCSKBench (Bisk et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023; Töberg et al., 2025) cover parts of it. Programming knowledge spans language semantics, data structures and algorithms, software interfaces, and the writing of short functions from specification. CodeMMLU (Nguyen et al., 2025) tests the first three, and the EvalPlus versions of HumanEval and MBPP (Liu et al., 2023c) test the last. In HumanEval and MBPP, the model completes small, self-contained function from its signature and description, and unit tests score the result. On robot, the same skill produces helpers such as function that converts detected bounding box into grasp point. Results should identify the categories tested and the scoring protocol. General physical-commonsense scores do not establish coverage of robot structure, sensing, or kinematics, which require explicit probes. Offline scores also characterize knowledge only under the chosen protocol; closed-loop competence requires separate system-level evaluation. Understanding. Understanding tests ask whether an S2 foundation model can extract an accurate, task-relevant representation of the world, the users goal, and the robots own state from available observations. Unlike knowledge tests, they concern particular physical situation. They cover multimodal perception, spatial and physical state estimation, affordance recognition, temporal understanding, task interpretation, recognition of human behavior, awareness of the robots body and of the skills and interfaces available to it, progress estimation, and uncertainty assessment. Table 2 lists these abilities with an evaluation target and candidate benchmarks for each. Two of them deserve particular weight because they matter for closed-loop control and are weak in current models. 22 Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems Understanding of the robots own body and capabilities tells S2 whether to delegate to skill or to act directly. Understanding of task progress and completion makes verification possible, yet success detectors are biased toward reporting success (Navasardyan et al., 2026). Static question answering also misses the temporal side of understanding: because observations age while S2 deliberates, model must distinguish what it observed, and when, from what still holds now. Finally, tests must respect the boundary with reasoning: understanding determines what is happening and what can be inferred, whereas reasoning determines what should be done next. For example, recognizing that an object has slipped from the gripper tests understanding; identifying the cause and selecting corrective action tests reasoning. Evaluating understanding therefore requires separating state inference from downstream decisionmaking and execution. At the model level, tests should specify the observations, task instructions, robot-state information, and interaction history available to the model. Such specification matters most for progress estimation and uncertainty assessment, where the correct answer may depend on earlier observations or on information that remains unobservable. At the system level, task outcomes provide complementary evidence, but they cannot by themselves attribute failures to understanding, because planning, tool use, and execution may also contribute. Together, these tests characterize the information quality on which S2 decisions depend. Whether the agent can use that information to select effective actions is the subject of reasoning evaluation. Reasoning tests ask whether the S2 foundation model can select and revise decisions that advance the users goal, given its understanding of the current state, the robots capabilities, and the constraints of the physical environment. They cover intent inference, causal and counterfactual prediction, hierarchical planning, spatial exploration, skill selection and orchestration, executable action inference, active perception and intervention decisions, failure recovery, and handling of interruptions and rescheduling. Executable action inference, which corresponds to the direct-control path of Figure 4, needs precise evaluation target. We treat it as reasoning ability rather than as separate policy dimension. The target is therefore whether the model produces physically executable, goal-consistent action decisions, not whether it can reliably control robot as complete policy. Reliable control also depends on continuous closed-loop operation, latency, controllers, and the harness, so it belongs to system-level evaluation. Distinguishing reasoning competence from execution performance requires tests at both levels. At the model level, controlled decision-making tests assess whether the model selects feasible, goal-consistent actions under specified observations, capabilities, and constraints, without physical execution. At the system level, closed-loop tests additionally assess whether its decisions remain effective when actions are executed and their outcomes are observed. The distinction matters because task success depends not only on decision quality but also on the harness, tools, controllers, and physical environment. Efficiency evaluation measures the latency from observation to action, the number of model calls, the freshness of the observations on which each decision rests (the observation age defined in Equation 1), and the rate of timeouts and missed deadlines, under stated reasoning budget and response deadline. Output tokens per second measure decoding speed, not robot responsiveness. Latency should therefore include perception, context preparation, inference, network delay, tool execution, and controller response whenever they are on the critical path. Cost should be reported as tokens, API charges, total task time, and robot occupancy, per attempt and per success, including failures and retries. Reported costs differ by orders of magnitude, and cost rankings need not follow success rankings. In Astranomy, an agentic Astra session used 30.9M tokens ($36.40) per successful episode, against 160k tokens ($1.96) for direct prompting, although most of its input was served from cache (Yang et al., 2026d). On RoboQuest, an average episode with Astra took 10.4 minutes of simulated time but 53.8 minutes of wall-clock time and cost $11.29 (Liu et al., 2026c). On single real six-axis arm, frontier coding agents took about 30 minutes per task that person completes in 20 seconds (Artificial Analysis, 2026). User Intent. For user intent, explicit instructions are the easy case; harder cases include vague requests, unstated preferences, learned habits, and changes of mind during task. Evaluation should therefore score the final state against the users intent rather than the literal instruction. It should also report the number of clarifying questions, adherence to stated and learned preferences, the handling of corrections and interruptions, and the number of human interventions. Existing benchmarks cover only parts of intent fulfillment. PRISM isolates implicit intent resolution, which was significant bottleneck for all model families (Lim et al., 2026). TEACh requires acting on intent conveyed over several dialogue turns (Padmakumar et al., 2022), and Ask-to-Act scores clarification of ambiguous requests (Ramrakhya et al., 2025). MEMENTO finds that agents can recall simple object semantics but struggle to apply sequential user patterns to planning (Kwon et al., 2026). Two devices can be borrowed from digital agents: hidden supervisor with simulated user who gives multi-turn feedback without leaking grading criteria (Chen et al., 2026e), and the pass𝑘 reliability metric (Yao et al., 2024). To our knowledge, no benchmark yet scores end-to-end intent fulfillment on real robots with real users across sessions. 4.2. How to Evaluate The dimensions above specify what to measure. Comparable results also require common way of measuring, which the same benchmark name does not guarantee. We therefore propose the following principles, several of which are adapted from the evaluation of digital agents (Yao et al., 2024; Kwa et al., 2025). i. Separate the model from the system. Fix the harness when comparing foundation models, and fix the model when comparing harnesses. In both cases, match the embodiment, interfaces, observations, task instances, and budgets. Otherwise, label the comparison as one between complete systems, as CodeActionBench does (Lyu et al., 2026). What counts as no tools must be defined by the interface contract rather than by name: in EmbodiedSkillBench, for example, the no skill condition still acts through registered native end-effector and gripper tools (Han et al., 2026). ii. Treat the action interface as controlled variable. The same foundation model may call skills, emit end-effector targets, or output joint targets (Figure 4). These interfaces do not form scale from easy to hard: each brings different execution priors, control burdens, failure modes, and degrees of freedom. Model comparisons should therefore fix the action abstraction level and report it. Its effect can be measured directly by holding the model, tasks, robot, sensors, environment, and budgets fixed while varying the interface. The comparison should include 29 Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems skill-only interface, direct end-effector interface, and hybrid in which the model decides when to call skill and when to act directly. Such comparisons should report task success separately from action validity, collisions and constraint violations, the number of calls, physical execution time, inference latency, recovery, and total cost. iii. Run on world clock. Many simulated evaluations pause the world while the model deliberates (Jedlicki et al., 2026; Galbot Team et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026j). Paused and live execution measure different abilities and must be reported separately. On matched hard routes of RT-Safe, live execution raised collisions by factor of 12.3 but left task completion essentially unchanged. Safe success fell from 19.8% to 0.7%, and mean latency was positively associated with collisions across models (Xu et al., 2026d). Embodied First Exam separates Standard setting, in which the agent receives sensor observations and the simulation pauses while it deliberates, from Realtime setting, in which the environment continues to advance during decision-making. On 54 dynamic core tasks evaluated in both settings, GPT-6 Astra solved 23 Standard tests and 17 Realtime tests (Wang et al., 2026d). Live evaluations should report the rate of missed deadlines and the distribution of the observation age. The age is defined as Δ𝑡obs = 𝑡effect 𝑡capture, (1) where 𝑡capture is when the observation behind decision was captured and 𝑡effect when the resulting action takes effect. Because it includes perception, communication, queuing, and execution delays, observation age reflects the physical response more closely than model inference latency does. When sensors, computation, and actuators run on different devices, both times must be measured on synchronized clocks. iv. Disclose the observation contract. State what the model and its tools receive: cameras and their history, the source of depth (a sensor, prediction, or triangulation), privileged object state, success or progress signals, and any demonstrations or scene assets. Give the agent only information that real robot could also obtain (OpenRUA Team, 2026). Without this disclosure, numbers from different studies cannot be compared. v. Verify completion independently. Decide success with checker that has access to ground truth that the system cannot observe, and never accept the models own claim or successful tool return as proof. Report the rate of false completion claims, because agents often declare success prematurely (Jedlicki et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026c) and VLM judges are biased toward success (Navasardyan et al., 2026). The checker must also be inaccessible to the agent. In one study, agents read static object files that physical robot could not read and located hidden success check within single session (Wang et al., 2026g). Hiding the verifier changes results substantially. When tool returns no longer revealed success, agents had to decide for themselves when an episode ended. Under this condition, the mean scores of two systems over 50 episodes on 10 tasks of RoboDojo fell from 83.2 to 63.5 and from 42.0 to 26.1 (OpenRUA Team, 2026). vi. Quantify uncertainty and reliability. Report per-task results, the number of repetitions, and confidence intervals. difference of few percentage points on handful of real-robot trials rarely supports conclusion (TRI LBM Team et al., 2025; Kress-Gazit et al., 2024). Reliability across repeated runs, such as the probability that all 𝑘 trials succeed, should complement the chance of at least one success (Yao et al., 2024). Rankings that aggregate benchmarks need the same care. The Robot Intelligence Index, for example, reports for each model the range within which its rank falls in 90% of resampled re-runs (Playground Research, 2026). vii. Control and sweep budgets. Fix and report the reasoning effort, the budgets for calls, steps, and wall-clock time, and any retry rules, and sweep them into successcost and successlatency curves where possible. In Astranomy, raising the effort from medium to extra-high improved success only from 72.7% to 74.5% at 2.6 times the latency and 2.2 times the cost (Yang et al., 2026d). Budgets must also match the benchmarks own limits: recounted under RoboDojos 30 Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems native step limit, one systems success rate fell from 47.1% to 1.0%, because 97 of its 99 successes came after that limit (OpenRUA Team, 2026). Improvement methods should be compared with retry baselines under the same budget, with development and test tasks kept apart (Wang et al., 2026j,g). For example, skill developed on one task with the benchmarks verifier raised that tasks score from 0 to 80 yet left two of four other tasks at baseline (OpenRUA Team, 2026). Results that use context about the test tasks should not be compared with zero-shot results (OpenRUA Team, 2026). viii. Validate on real robots. Treat simulation as screen rather than verdict, and audit the shortcuts of shared simulated suites. In SIMPLER, simulated success tracked real success closely once control and visual gaps to the real setup were mitigated, and less closely when they were only partly mitigated (Li et al., 2025a). Policies trained in simulation can also fail badly on real robots (Ibarz et al., 2021). Real-robot evaluations should pair seeds and scenes and report the human assistance and environment resets they required. ix. Fix the conditions of level claim in advance. Some results are offered as evidence that robot carries level of delegated responsibility (Section 6.1). Such result should fix beforehand the initial conditions, the permitted assistance and interruptions and how they are counted, and the evidence of completion. Completing long script does not demonstrate delegation if person must keep repairing the plan. The duration of the work should be measured in the time that skilled person would need for it, as METR (Kwa et al., 2025) does for software agents. The robots own wall-clock time and the human assistance it received should be reported separately, because robot may need far longer than person for the same work. The checklist below collects the information that these principles require every report to disclose. Reporting Checklist: The Harness Card. Every reported S2 result should be accompanied by harness card. The card records (i) the foundation model, its version, and its reasoning budget, and (ii) the harness version, prompts, skill library, memory, and verifiers. It records (iii) the embodiment and the S1 and S0 interfaces, with the action abstraction and control rates, and (iv) the observation contract and any privileged information. It also records (v) the time semantics, that is, whether the world pauses during inference, and (vi) the number of runs and seeds, with confidence intervals. Finally, it records (vii) the rate and definition of human or rule-based interventions and the paths for cancellation and human takeover. 4.3. Current evidence does not support cross-paper rankings, because interfaces, privileged information, budgets, and time semantics differ. Nor does it support claims of reliability, because many headline results come from single runs or few seeds. Aggregate rankings have begun to address the first problem. The Robot Intelligence Index, launched with 16 public simulated and real-robot benchmarks and extended to 22 by November 4, 2026, combines them into one rating per model using weighted BradleyTerry model. In this model, benchmarks weight is the independence of its evaluators multiplied by the repeatability of its scores (Playground Research, 2026). The index itself shows, however, why single rating cannot replace the profile we recommend: 13 of the 23 models that rank in the top three on some benchmark rank in the bottom half on another. Performance in the real world, in continuous time, and over long horizons also remains largely unmeasured, including memory across sessions and the fulfillment of user intent on real robots. Several further findings rest on single study so far. One is that common embodied-reasoning benchmarks did not track closed-loop control (Yang et al., 2026b); another is that, when the world changes, memory fails mainly at replacing outdated state rather than at retaining history (Liang et al., 2026a). Digital Agents versus Physical Agents Agentic robotics inherits central principle from digital agents: foundation model can solve complex tasks by repeatedly observing an environment, invoking tools, and verifying the results. Its architecture, foundation model in loop with tools, context, and memory, draws on two lineages. One is digital agents, which have advanced rapidly on coding, computer use, and research tasks; the other is earlier work on robots driven by language models. The success of digital agents, however, rests on favorable properties of the digital world: interfaces that the model reads and writes directly, 36 Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems outcomes that can be checked automatically, abundant data, and environments that are cheap to copy and reset. Physical environments weaken each of these properties and add constraints of time, irreversibility, and embodiment. The challenge is therefore not to give digital agent cameras and robotic tools, but to determine which assumptions no longer hold, which principles still transfer, and what must be rebuilt for reliable physical execution. Our answer is that the principles of digital agents largely transfer, but the assumptions that make them reliable do not. We first review what digital agents can do and why, and then take up these three questions in turn. 5.1. What Digital Agents Can Do and Why The length of software tasks that frontier agents can complete has grown steadily. METR (Kwa et al., 2025) measures this progress as time horizon: the duration, in human working time, of tasks that an agent completes with given probability. The horizon has doubled roughly every seven months since 2019 (Kwa et al., 2025; METR, 2026a), and about every four months since 2023 on METRs revised task suite (METR, 2026a). By 2026, the best measured 50% horizons exceeded ten hours, and METR cautions that measurements above 16 hours are unreliable with its current task suite (METR, 2026b). These results measure capability on particular distributions of software tasks with checkable specifications, not reliable long-horizon autonomy in general. Reliable completion is harder: time horizons at 80% success are several times shorter than at 50% (Kwa et al., 2025; METR, 2026b). digital agent pairs foundation model with harness of tools, context management, memory, and an execution sandbox. Its results benefit from four conditions that software happens to satisfy. We call them enabling conditions: they recur across the systems behind much of the recent progress, and we treat them as design guidance. First, the interface is native to the model: state and actions take the form of the models own inputs and outputs. State is text that the agent reads, and actions are text or code that it emits directly through an agentcomputer interface (Yang et al., 2024). Outcomes are generally verifiable: compilers, tests, and program execution return objective signals quickly and at scale, signals that support iteration at test time (Yang et al., 2024) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (Lambert et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). Data are abundant: public code, documentation, and discussion accumulated over decades give pretrained models broad knowledge of the domain; Codex, for example, was trained on code from 54 million public GitHub repositories (Chen et al., 2021). Environments are cheap: sandbox with an executable runtime and unit tests can be copied, run in parallel, reset, and replayed, so that agents can be trained and evaluated on thousands of real tasks (Pan et al., 2025). The first two conditions shape every step of the agents loop; the last two determine how much the agent can learn before deployment and how widely it can be tested. Wei (2025) links verification to learning through verifiers rule: the ease of training AI to solve task is proportional to how verifiable the task is. Because these conditions are properties of task setting rather than of programming per se, capability has spread to settings in which they could be established. These settings include software engineering (Jimenez et al., 2024) and professional work across many occupations (Patwardhan et al., 2025). They also include computer use, in which agents operate graphical interfaces in real operating systems (Xie et al., 2024), and visual coding, in which generated code is rendered and compared with design or specification (Si et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026e). Most recently, they include 3D content, in which agents write programs for modeling software and game engines (Gao et al., 2026c; Ye et al., 2026b). Most of these extensions weaken some of the conditions, and capability lags where they weaken. Computer use weakens the native interface by replacing text with pixels and clicks. Its time horizons are 40 to 100 times shorter than those in software and reasoning domains, although they are increasing at similar rates (Kwa and Cheng, 2025). Outcomes are not automatically verifiable. Digital-agent design usually assumes that outcomes can be checked automatically, quickly, and reproducibly. By the verifiers rule (Wei, 2025), this scarcity of credible verification is itself central obstacle to training physical agents. The resulting problem is to verify outcomes using evidence: each verdict must state which of the four questions of the agentic loop it answers (acceptance, termination, physical effect, or intent) and come from calibrated verifier. Data are not abundant. Digital-agent design assumes that pretraining has already covered the domain. Unlike natural language and two-dimensional vision, dexterous manipulation has no Internet-scale corpus (Hoque et al., 2025). Robot data are produced by operating robots, at the pace of the physical world. The 76,000 trajectories of DROID, about 350 hours of interaction, took 50 data collectors twelve months on three continents (Khazatsky et al., 2024). Teleoperation of this kind lacks scale and diversity, and synthetic data bring gap to reality (Luo et al., 2025). Human video scales more easily, but large collections such as Ego4D (Grauman et al., 2022) lack native hand-pose annotations and action labels (Hoque et al., 2025), and video records no contact forces. Touch is scarcest: acquiring large-scale and reliable tactile data in the physical world remains costly (Chen et al., 2026a). The resulting problem is one of supply: abundant data must be manufactured by data engine that turns the operation of robots into training data. Environments are not cheap to copy and reset. Digital-agent design assumes that environments can be copied, reset, and run in parallel. Where simulation is faithful, the digital recipe returns: with thousands of simulated robots trained in parallel, quadruped learns to walk on uneven terrain in about twenty minutes (Rudin et al., 2022). Where it is not, policies trained in simulation often fail to transfer to the real world (Tan et al., 2018), and simulation pipelines have only begun to cover complex physics such as deformable objects and fluids (Qin et al., 2026c). The alternative, practice in the real world, requires the scene to be reset after each attempt; this is typically handled by automated reset skills, with manual reset as fallback when automatic reset fails (Li et al., 2026d). The cheap, parallel, and resettable environment of digital agents therefore exists only in part. The resulting problem is twofold: every physical experiment has cost that must be budgeted, and results obtained in simulation must be validated against reality. What Transfers Beneath the practices that make digital agents work lie principles about how an agent organizes its work, not about what its environment provides. Because they do not depend on the enabling conditions, five such principles carry over to physical agents and already shape our architecture. Close the loop on evidence. Agents are language models using tools based on environmental feedback in loop and need ground truth from the environment at each step (Anthropic, 2024a). For robot, the principle requires the agent to observe and assess an actions relevant effects before treating its intended outcome as established or making decision that depends on that outcome. The agent may continue planning or monitoring while an action is in progress, provided that subsequent actions respect the execution and safety constraints. Treat tools as contracts. Tools are contracts between deterministic systems and non-deterministic agents (Anthropic, 2025d). Execution contracts extend this principle to physical calls. capability contract, for example, states skills inputs and units, preconditions, expected effects, time limits, and behavior on cancellation, so that S2 can reason about call before making it and interpret its result afterward. Manage context explicitly, and keep durable state outside it. Context is finite resource with diminishing returns, managed through compaction, structured notes, and sub-agents (Anthropic, 2025a). Long-running agents also keep progress files (Anthropic, 2025b) and session log outside the models context window (Anthropic, 2026b). The embodied harness applies the same discipline to the world, the user, and the body: it keeps task progress, maps, and memories outside the model and supplies them when decision requires them. Separate doing from judging. Long-running agents benefit from end-to-end tests, because models tend to mark work as complete without proper testing (Anthropic, 2025b). Separating the agent that performs the work from the agent that judges it also helps (Anthropic, 2026a). In the embodied harness, the verifier is the judge: it assesses each step and the task from evidence rather than from the models claim that it has finished. Package capabilities as reusable skills. Digital agents load packaged skills when task needs them (Anthropic, 2025c). An agent in Minecraft accumulated library of skills written as code (Wang et al., 2024a). For robots, S1 skills and the programs that S2 writes play this role (Figure 4): capability validated once can be invoked many times, and reuse also reduces the number of decisions that S2 must make at run time. Foundations. Four foundations replace the four enabling conditions. Grounded state and action interfaces in place of native interface. On the state side, the harness maintains belief state: persistent and revisable estimate of world, user, and body state. Road Ahead Agentic robotics broadens the question by which progress in robotics is judged: from what robot can do on command to what it can be entrusted to do on its own. General foundation models already supply much of the knowledge and reasoning that such trust requires. Turning these capabilities into dependable physical work, however, raises problems of timing, persistent state, verification, 43 Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems adaptation, and learning from experience that no single model release will resolve. Where the field goes next will therefore depend on how it measures progress and which of these problems it addresses. This section proposes ladder of delegable work as measure of progress and places current systems on it. It then identifies research directions that climbing the ladder requires and closes with open questions about how agentic robotic systems should be built. 6.1. Reaching embodied intelligence that is genuinely useful calls for high-level ladder that guides progress toward it. We propose such ladder for agentic robotics: it measures progress by the scope of responsibility that robot can reliably carry alone, independently of its body, domain, or implementation. The ladder has four levels (Figure 12). At L1, the primitive level, the robot executes local skill, such as picking up cup, and checks whether the intended result has been achieved. At L2, the task level, the robot coordinates skills to deliver complete task, such as making and serving coffee: Embodied S2 decomposes the goal, selects actions, monitors execution, and responds to failures until the acceptance criteria are met. At L3, the workflow level, the robot coordinates interdependent tasks toward an overall goal, such as preparing breakfast for four: Embodied S2 manages timing, priorities, and shared resources, and revises its plan as needed. At L4, the role level, the robot sustains an agreed responsibility across successive tasks and workflows, such as managing daily breakfast around household schedules and preferences. This responsibility continues after individual workflows end, until it expires or is withdrawn. Each level builds on those below it, extending the scope over which the robot must connect reasoning, execution, and verification. Spatial scope and complexity complement the ladder: within each level, progress means reliably fulfilling the delegated responsibility across broader environments and more demanding activities. As the operating scope expands from workcell to room, building, or site (Figure 13 and Table 11), robots must integrate observations across locations, remember relevant objects and events, and seek information beyond their immediate view. These demands, like those of complex activities, fall on Embodied S2, which maintains goals and context while guiding action through the loop of observation, reasoning, execution, and verification. We therefore expect the value of agentic robotics to grow with scope and complexity. Embodied Reasoning Under Physical Constraints S2 must understand the world, anticipate the consequences of its actions, and decide within limited time and computation, yet current S2 foundation models fall short in both speed and decision quality. With frontier model as its S2 foundation model, S2 decides once every several to forty seconds (Xu et al., 2026d; Yang et al., 2026d; Galbot Team et al., 2026), far slower than the S1 skills it directs (Figure 8). More deliberation helps when the world waits (Gemini Robotics Team, 2025b) but hurts when it moves (Xu et al., 2026d). Decisions remain weak where embodiment matters most: judging success from ambiguous evidence (Navasardyan et al., 2026), anticipating the consequences of actions (Sun et al., 2026a), and deciding when to stop exploring (Liu et al., 2026c). We therefore advocate making capped scaling an explicit training and system objective: maximizing decision quality subject to response deadline, evaluated without pausing the world and reported as successlatencycost curves. Three questions follow. First, when is further reasoning worth its time, and when should the robot observe again or act at once? Second, which decisions must be made online, and which can be reused or turned into skills? Partial answers to both include routing each subtask to planner of appropriate strength (Dao et al., 2026) and launching chains of primitives with one call (Xu et al., 2026a). fast policy can also consult frontier model only for recovery (Sun et al., 2026b), and authoring skills offline removes the slow model from the loop (Bai et al., 2026). However, current harnesses are built and evaluated almost entirely on single tasks in workcell or room (Section 4.4). Three questions stand out. The first is how to represent and maintain state that spans rooms, floors, and days, so that the robot knows what it still knows. Candidates include augmenting spatially 46 Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems grounded scene graphs with outcomes learned through interaction (Banwasi et al., 2026) and recording subgoal as complete only after evidence of completion (Zhao et al., 2026a). The second is how to coordinate the interdependent tasks of workflow, which share information, resources, and deadlines. The third is how to divide judgment between the model and the execution system: which checks belong inside skills and verifiers, and which decisions must return to S2. Yet current success remains highly dependent on the specific embodiment (Section 4.1). We advocate three lines of work. The first is reuse of knowledge and experience: in-context adaptation and skill libraries of validated repairs reduce what must be learned anew (Lu et al., 2026), and compiled skills can be frozen and carried to other agents (Bai et al., 2026). The second is capability interfaces, such as capability cards and device descriptions, that let S2 plan for body it has not used before. The third is skill adaptation: in one study, single policy, conditioned on examples of commanded actions and resulting motions, adapted in context to unseen controller modes and gains (Yang et al., 2026e). Continual Improvement from Physical Experience robot holding role for weeks keeps meeting new tasks and changes in its environment and body that no training run anticipates. It must therefore learn from physical experience which object properties, user preferences, causes of failure, and skills are worth keeping. We distinguish three kinds of change. Adaptation adjusts behavior to the current task, environment, or feedback. Continual improvement retains change to memory, tools, skills, the harness, or policy, and verifies that it improves later work. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) improves the process that produces such changes, making subsequent improvement more effective. Robots have long improved through autonomous data collection, learned rewards, and reinforcement learning, and DrEureka used language models to design reward functions and domain randomization for sim-to-real transfer (Ma et al., 2024b). What recent agentic systems add, mostly around frozen foundation models, is loop that diagnoses failures from operating experience and revises the system, usually with foundation model proposing the revisions (Tian et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026e; Deng et al., 2026). This loop starts with attribution: deciding whether failure came from perception, planning, skill, or an interface, which part should change, and why the change should help future tasks.
