Conclusion Agentic robotics organizes capabilities around user intent through closed loop of reasoning, action, verification, and adaptation. Our reference framework distinguishes three complementary functional roles: System 2 (S2) for goal-directed reasoning and decision-making, System 1 (S1) for executable skills, and System 0 (S0) for low-level control. S2 can invoke S1 skills or issue commands directly to 48 Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems S0. We refer to its realization through foundation model and an embodied harness as Embodied S2, the decision-making core that connects general-purpose intelligence with embodied execution. Four ideas underpin this perspective. First, foundation models make S2 promising starting point for robot generalization. Their broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities can help robots understand unfamiliar goals and situations, organize available capabilities, and adapt through feedback. This offers complementary path to improving action policies through larger and more diverse training datasets. Second, physical autonomy requires the model and embodied harness to jointly support effective, verifiable action under constraints of time, embodiment, uncertainty, and safety. These constraints must shape how systems reason, execute, and adapt. Third, meaningful evaluation must distinguish model capabilities from closed-loop system performance while examining how those capabilities contribute to reliable outcomes. Finally, the long-term objective is sustained autonomy with progressively broader responsibility, extending from individual primitives and tasks to coordinated workflows and standing roles. Realizing this ambition requires robots to track goals and progress over time, coordinate interdependent activities, recover from failures, and adapt to changing environments and embodiments. Improvement from physical experience must carry over to subsequent work while preserving existing capabilities. The evidence reviewed here does not yet establish reliable autonomy across these broader and more persistent responsibilities, making sustained performance central target for both system development and evaluation. This work calls for three community priorities. First, develop reliable evaluation frameworks that complement simulation with real-robot testing and extend task coverage to higher levels of responsibility and broader spatial scopes. Evaluation should assess sustained performance under changing conditions, including recovery from failure. Second, improve reasoning efficiency for time-sensitive, safety-critical, and highly dynamic settings. When test-time scaling relies on longer deliberation, gains in reasoning quality may come at the cost of timely action. Research should therefore prioritize better decisions within the time available for action, with the longer-term goal of developing embodied-native reasoning that integrates perception, reasoning, and action in response to the dynamics and urgency of physical tasks. Third, standardize reporting of the model, harness, available capabilities, evaluation conditions, inference budgets, response times, and human assistance. Clear reporting supports reproducible comparisons and helps distinguish model capabilities from the support provided by the surrounding system. Together, these priorities can help turn promising results into credible progress toward sustained physical autonomy. We envision new era of robotic systems that understand human intent, adapt to changing circumstances, and reliably take on broader responsibilities over longer time horizons. Agentic robotics offers system-level path toward this vision, bringing the general-purpose capabilities of foundation models into systems that people can trust with sustained work in the physical world. 49 Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems A. HexaShell runs thin harness with tools written and tested by optimizer agents (Gao et al., 2026b); later version uses small set of 14 general tools (Gao et al., 2026a). Others maintain persistent playbooks (Lee et al., 2026b). General-purpose agents drive physical robots directly (Jia et al., 2026) and learn in context from demonstrations (Cheng et al., 2026). One study argues that, given the right interface, coding and computer-use agents are in sense already robot-control agents (Hu et al., 2026a). Orchestration frameworks connect agents to ROS 2 and to learned skills and policies (Li et al., 2026d; Cardenas et al., 2026; Galanti et al., 2026), and other methods reduce how often the expensive model is consulted (Sun et al., 2026b; Xu et al., 2026a). Our Position. These systems implement all or part of the S2 loop through layered orchestration, direct control, or code as policy (Figure 4). We identify S2 by its decisions, not its interface, and treat verification, persistent context, and revision as part of S2. From these works we draw comparisons that fix the model or the harness, and we report cost and time semantics alongside success. A.3. Hierarchical and Dual-System Robot Foundation Models Many robot foundation models separate high-level reasoning from low-level action. Helix pairs slow vision-language model with fast visuomotor policy that receives latent vector (Figure AI, 2025b), and Helix 02 adds learned whole-body controller (Figure AI, 2026a). GR00T N1 couples vision-language module with diffusion action module trained end to end (NVIDIA et al., 2025c). In Hi Robot, high-level VLM chooses the next step for low-level policy (Shi et al., 2025). The 𝜋0 model follows commands from high-level VLM (Black et al., 2025b), and 𝜋0.5 co-trains subtask prediction with action generation (Black et al., 2025a). Gemini Robotics 1.5 interleaves naturallanguage reasoning with actions and is paired in an agentic system with an embodied reasoning model, Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5, that acts as orchestrator (Gemini Robotics Team, 2025b). Other dual-system designs use value-guided sampling (Song et al., 2025), combine generalist with specialist policy (Bu et al., 2024), or embed the fast system inside the slow one (Chen et al., 2025a). Still others switch adaptively between reasoning and acting (Lin et al., 2025) or communicate through 2D paths (Li et al., 2025b) and editable trajectory traces (Lee et al., 2025). Unified models generate reasoning and actions with one decoder (Liu et al., 2026e) or within one tightly coupled mixture-of-experts model (Zhai et al., 2025). Recent work adds world-model-guided test-time search to subtask generation (Cai et al., 2026) and studies design principles for hierarchical VLAs (Hu et al., 2026b). One study finds that the executor of hierarchical VLA underuses its plans (Xie et al., 2026). Our Position. We identify S2 by its decisions, not by its place in hierarchy: module acts as S2 only if it makes identifiable decisions on how to proceed and on outcomes. An upper module that 52 Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems emits only latent representation may perform this function, but we do not classify it as S2 unless replacement experiments reveal these decisions. The subtask stage of unified model, by contrast, makes an identifiable decision on how to proceed and so implements part of S2. That executors can underuse their plans suggests that S1s adherence to them should be measured. A.4. Embodied Reasoning Models family of models aims to supply the embodied reasoning that S2 needs. The Gemini Robotics-ER line introduced the ERQA benchmark and has evolved from reasoning model into an orchestrator of VLAs (Gemini Robotics Team, 2025a,b; Hansen and Xu, 2026). Cosmos-Reason1 trains physical common sense and embodied reasoning with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (NVIDIA et al., 2025b). Vesta combines generalist model with multimodal memory harness (Bjorck et al., 2026). RoboBrain models cover planning, affordance, and trajectory prediction (Ji et al., 2025; BAAI RoboBrain Team et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2026). Embodied-R1 uses pointing as an embodiment-agnostic interface, and Embodied-R1.5 adds closed plannergroundercorrector loop (Yuan et al., 2026c,d). Other models vary in scale and training recipe: RynnBrain (Dang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b), PhysBrain (DeepCybo Team et al., 2026), MiMo-Embodied (Hao et al., 2025), HY-Embodied (Tencent Robotics et al., 2026), Robix (Fang et al., 2025), ACE-Brain (ACE-Brain Team et al., 2026), Pelican-VL (Zhang et al., 2025b), and the MolmoER backbone of MolmoAct2 (Fang et al., 2026). Related spatial-grounding models include SpatialVLM, RoboPoint, RoboRefer, and Magma (Chen et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2025b; Zhou et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2025a). Vlaser studies how VLM initialization affects VLA fine-tuning (Yang et al., 2026b). Progress estimation can be framed as temporal ordering of shuffled frames (Ma et al., 2025). Recent models also train on data with execution feedback, goal revisions, and failure recovery (Foundation Model, Li Auto Inc, 2026; Li et al., 2026a). Our Position. Reports on these models mostly evaluate offline question answering, pointing, and spatial skills. We treat such model as candidate S2 foundation model whose value for the S2 loop must be shown at the system level. A.5. Agent Harnesses Digital Precedents. ReAct interleaved reasoning and acting (Yao et al., 2023), Toolformer taught models to call APIs (Schick et al., 2023), and Reflexion stored verbal feedback in episodic memory instead of updating weights (Shinn et al., 2023). Generative agents introduced memory streams with reflection and retrieval (Park et al., 2023), and CodeAct used executable Python as unified action space (Wang et al., 2024b). SWE-agent showed that the agentcomputer interface affects agent performance (Yang et al., 2024), and OpenHands provided an open sandboxed platform (Wang et al., 2025a). OSWorld benchmarked computer use (Xie et al., 2024). Computer-use models and the Model Context Protocol gave agents general ways to reach software (Anthropic, 2024b,c). As caution, automatic harness evolution can fail to outperform simple test-time scaling at matched budget (Wang et al., 2026j). Physical Harnesses. Thea adapts the coding-agent harness to robots, adding scene graph as context and exit codes that report action outcomes (Wang et al., 2026e). Runtime governance layers add policy checks, admission, monitoring, rollback, and human override (Qin et al., 2026b). PhyAgentOS separates execution termination from semantic completion (Liu et al., 2026d), and in one study of LLM-controlled devices, scoped capability tokens rejected every capability-escalation call that JSONschema validation let through (Yang, 2026). Harnesses with execution contracts and verification include DynaHarness, RegenHarness, SCOPERs harness, and harness for safe robot control (Deng 53 Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c; Wei et al., 2026a; Xu et al., 2026b). Programs serve as evolvable interfaces (Wang et al., 2026f), critics run on separate timescales (Ding et al., 2026), and frozen VLAs become retryable primitives (Zhang et al., 2026f). Navigation and persistence harnesses validate planner proposals (Chen et al., 2026c), support lifelong sessions (Zhao et al., 2026b), and carry user and scene context across sessions (Wang et al., 2026l). Our Position. We count the harness, that is, the non-model components that assemble the context for S2s decisions, carry them out, and verify their outcomes, as part of Embodied S2 rather than as layer around the model. Harness cards disclose its configuration so that system-level results can be attributed. A.6. Memory and World Models Explicit world memories for robots include open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs (Gu et al., 2024), retrieval-augmented spatiotemporal memory (Anwar et al., 2025), memory snapshots for exploration (Yang et al., 2025d), and combined longand short-term memories (Wang et al., 2025b). Policies can instead carry memory internally (Shi et al., 2026; Torne et al., 2026). User and long-term context remains less developed: in one study, agents struggled to apply sequential user patterns to planning (Kwon et al., 2026). Recent harnesses keep memories of people and preferences (Jin et al., 2026) and record the outcomes of interactions in the scene graph (Banwasi et al., 2026). In one manufacturing study, an external world-state model improved state tracking (Tang et al., 2026). Predictive world models have progressed from learned simulators (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2025) to generative interactive environments (Bruce et al., 2024; Google DeepMind, 2025), physical-AI platforms (NVIDIA et al., 2025a; NVIDIA, 2026), and self-supervised video world models used for planning (Assran et al., 2025). They increasingly enter the decision and evaluation loop, both for imagination-based search (Zhang et al., 2026d) and for evaluating policies (Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025). Criteria have also been proposed for when their verdicts can count as evidence (Oefinger et al., 2026). Our Position. We treat cross-session world, user, and body state as harness responsibility: each item records when and how it was obtained and can be revised. World models supply evidence for S2 but make neither kind of S2 decision, so they do not act as S2. A.7. Benchmarks Embodied benchmarks range from instruction following in simulated homes (Shridhar et al., 2020) and suites of manipulation tasks (Liu et al., 2023b; Zhou et al., 2025c; Li et al., 2024a) to realto-sim evaluation (Li et al., 2025a) and crowdsourced real-world evaluation (Atreya et al., 2025). Benchmarks for embodied agents and S2 include EmbodiedBench, the Embodied Agent Interface, VLABench, RoboCerebra, VSI-Bench, RoboBench, and ASIMOV (Yang et al., 2025c; Li et al., 2024b; Zhang et al., 2025a; Han et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b; Luo et al., 2026b; Sermanet et al., 2025). Closed-loop benchmarks from 2026 include RoboDojo for manipulation policies (Chen et al., 2026b) and RobotWorld, SCOPER, LIBERO-Agent, and CodeActionBench for agents (Yang et al., 2026j; Wei et al., 2026a; Diao et al., 2026; Lyu et al., 2026). Embodied First Exam evaluates coding agents across diverse simulated robots and tasks, allowing them to use direct control, generated programs, or trained policies under different protocols (Wang et al., 2026d). Other studies test the reliability of success detectors, runtime monitors, and safety refusals under robot control (Navasardyan et al., 2026; Ahmedt-Aristizabal et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026a). Section 4 discusses many of these benchmarks. 54 Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems Our Position. Many benchmarks evaluate the model alone or the whole stack without stating which. Few fix S1 and vary S2 (Han et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026a), and few score verification directly; exceptions include FailBench (Navasardyan et al., 2026), RESCUE (Ahmedt-Aristizabal et al., 2026), and the completion-claim accuracy of CodeActionBench (Lyu et al., 2026). We therefore evaluate at two levels, model and system, with harness card for every result. A.8. Self-Improvement and Continual Learning Before 2025, robots improved through autonomous data collection and relabeling (Xiao et al., 2023; Bousmalis et al., 2023; Ahn et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025d) and through reward functions written by language models (Ma et al., 2024a). Weight-level improvement of S1 policies now uses learned progress signals (Ghasemipour et al., 2025), reinforcement learning from experience (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025), fleet learning during deployment (Wang et al., 2026i), and agentic loops that verify rollouts and refine policies (Liu et al., 2026a; Xiao et al., 2026). Orchestrators and policies can co-evolve (Zhang et al., 2026e). Around frozen foundation models, systems revise tools, skills, and harnesses (Tian et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026h; Lu et al., 2026; Elmaaroufi et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026a), and some co-evolve policy, curriculum, and judge (Zhou et al., 2026b). Some results are cautionary. In one simulation study, accepted changes kept passing their tests while the target task never succeeded (Wang, 2026). In another, accepting every proposed revision degraded harness, whereas championchallenger rule improved it (Wei et al., 2026b). In third, continual-learning gains did not grow with more samples (Huang et al., 2026a). Our Position. Whereas S2 adapts to verified outcomes within task, claim of improvement asserts that retained change helps later work. Such claim should pass the three-part test of Section 6.2.4: gains on held-out tasks, no regression, and separate contributions of the S2 foundation model, the harness, and S1. This test is stricter than the standard of most current reports but weaker than the recursive-gain criterion of physical recursive self-improvement (Zhou et al., 2026a). B. Applications: What Agentic Robotics Changes Embodied S2 could expand the range of work that robots undertake and improve how reliably and efficiently they complete it. For each of several representative domains, we ask what earlier approaches already deliver, where they stop, what Embodied S2 could add, and how far reported deployments reach. Two earlier approaches set the baseline. Programmed automation, from industrial arms to warehouse systems, executes engineered motions and rules with high speed and precision, but only where the environment and the task are fixed in advance. Each new product, layout, or exception requires engineering effort. Learned policies, including VLA models, generalize across objects and scenes within the skills on which they were trained, and now complete whole tasks in homes they have never seen (Black et al., 2025a; Figure AI, 2026b). Each new task, however, still requires demonstrations, and policy does not by itself decide which task to do next, check that the result is correct, or recover when it is not. In reported deployments, these responsibilities fall to remote experts and operators: human backup performs the role of S2, pattern that recurs across the domains below. If Embodied S2 took over these responsibilities, three changes would follow. First, robot could be given new work by instruction rather than by reprogramming or new demonstrations, which would make automation worthwhile for varied, low-volume tasks that never justified the engineering. Second, robot could verify its own results and handle routine exceptions, so that one person could supervise many robots by exception instead of guiding one. Third, robot could carry state across Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems tasks and days, prerequisite for entrusting it with workflow or role rather than single task. We state the reach of each domain on the ladder of delegable work (Section 6.1; Figure 1), from single primitive (L1) through task (L2) and workflow (L3) to standing role (L4). Because people still fill much of the role of S2, human interventions per task, or per shift for continuous operations, should become standard deployment metric alongside reliability and execution efficiency. Table 13 summarizes the reports and our assessment for each domain. B.1. Homes Homes are the most numerous and the least structured of these settings. Single-purpose appliances such as robot vacuum cleaners work reliably because their task is fixed. General-purpose home robots are now emerging. Figure AI reports 56% whole-task success in 30 unseen homes in company-run evaluation that counts any rollout requiring safety intervention as failure (Figure AI, 2026b). Consumer humanoids are offered for sale, although their shipping volumes have not been disclosed. According to its manufacturer, the 1X NEO is sold with remote supervision by company expert for chores that the robot cannot yet perform alone (1X Technologies, 2026). An assessment by MIT Technology Review noted that the robot still needs remote operator for most tasks (Condliffe, 2026). Reported home autonomy thus reaches L2, the task level, and remote operation bridges the rest. Much of what the remote operator supplies is the work of S2. request such as get the living room ready for guests, but leave the childrens puzzle on the table leaves most objects, all steps, and the completion criterion unstated. Fulfilling it requires interpreting what the household wants, deciding where each item belongs, sequencing the work, checking the result, and responding to interruptions. Throughout, the robot must remember the home, its occupants, and their preferences while protecting their privacy. An Embodied S2 that handled such requests would change what home robot is. It would no longer be an appliance for one chore or teleoperated body, but helper to which household delegates an open list of chores. Remote experts would then approve exceptions rather than perform the work. B.2. Manufacturing and Logistics Factories and warehouses are where robots already work at large scale (International Federation of Robotics, 2026; Dresser, 2025), and where the limits of programmed automation are most visible. Industrial arms repeat engineered motions with high speed and precision inside fixtures and cells. This approach pays off in high-volume production but turns every change of product or layout into an engineering project. Humanoids and learned policies are now entering these settings. Figure AI reports that its Figure 02 deployment at BMW ran ten-hour shifts and contributed to the production of more than 30,000 vehicles (Figure AI, 2025a). Apptronik agreed to pilot its Apollo humanoid at Mercedes-Benz, runs data collection at customer sites including Mercedes-Benz, and uses the resulting fleet data to train Gemini Robotics models (Apptronik, 2024, 2026; Gemini Robotics Team, 2025a). Hyundai has announced plans to deploy Boston Dynamics Atlas in its plants (Boston Dynamics, 2026b). Skild AI reports more than 60 paying customers ten months after its first commercial deployment; mobility accounts for 10% of its revenue, and the remaining 90% comes mainly from manipulation tasks (Pathak and Gupta, 2026). In logistics, Agility reports that its Digit robots have moved more than 100,000 totes at GXO (Agility Robotics, 2025; GXO Logistics and Agility Robotics, 2026). Amazon reports operating more than million robots coordinated by what it describes as fleet foundation model (Dresser, 2025), and its tactile picking robot asks human workers to take over items that it cannot handle (Davies, 2025). All of these figures are company-reported. Because each cycle in these settings is short and repetitive, Embodied S2 would contribute less 56 Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems Table 13 Application domains: what earlier approaches deliver, what Embodied S2 could add, and the reach reported so far. Needed: Primitive (agriculture; manufacturer reports); task to workflow per trip, in restricted domains (mobility; company reports). It could verify each cycle and handle exceptions such as jam or an unfamiliar item, diagnosing the cause and then either retrying differently or handing over with precise report. It could also orchestrate fleets and re-task robots when production changes. Re-tasking may bring the largest gain. An Embodied S2 that composed existing skills into new sequence from work instruction, and verified the first parts before running at volume, would turn reprogramming project into configuration step. Automation could then extend from high-volume lines to high-mix, low-volume work that fixed automation has rarely reached. B.3. Inspection Inspection is an early commercial application of embodied reasoning models, which are candidate S2 foundation models. It suits current models because it tolerates latency and rewards verified reading of physical state, and it illustrates the step from collecting data to making judgments. conventional inspection robot repeats preplanned route and records data for people to interpret. Boston Dynamics reports more than 1,500 Spot robots with customers (Boston Dynamics, 2026c) and has integrated Gemini Robotics-ER into its inspection software for reading gauges and interpreting site conditions (Graesser and Xu, 2026; Boston Dynamics, 2026a). Google reports demonstration in which Gemini 4 Argon controls real Spot after practicing the task in simulated twin that it built itself (Rao, 2026). An Embodied S2 could connect reading and control by acting on what it reads. When gauge is out of range, it could look again from another angle, check the related valve, and file report with the evidence attached, instead of leaving every anomaly for person to find in the recordings. At the role level, inspection would also require persistent model of the site that is updated on every round. B.4. Healthcare and Laboratories Hospital delivery robots already navigate elevators and corridors autonomously (Diligent Robotics, 2024), but they carry items between fixed points. An Embodied S2 could turn such robot into an assistant for varied requests, such as fetching particular item from supply room. Eldercare is the most demanding domain considered here. Delegating it to robot would require responsibility at the role level (L4), long-term memory of person, well-timed intervention, and the strongest privacy and safety protections. Current evidence is limited to trials. Laboratory automation has long executed fixed protocols, and structured laboratories also host autonomous research campaigns that run continuously for days. The A-Lab synthesized 36 of 57 target compounds over 17 days of continuous operation (Szymanski et al., 2023), although the novelty of its products and the automated analysis that identified them were later disputed; the count given here is the corrected one (Leeman et al., 2024; Szymanski et al., 2026). mobile robotic chemist ran 688 experiments over eight days (Burger et al., 2020). These runs show sustained operation in restricted domain rather than role held across open-ended work. language-model agent, Coscientist, has also planned and executed chemistry experiments (Boiko et al., 2023). In open-ended work, an Embodied S2 could decide which experiment to run next given the results so far, verify that each step produced what it should, and record provenance. In laboratories, verification of outcomes, rather than manipulation, is likely to be the bottleneck. B.5. Agriculture and Mobility Agricultural robots operate commercially at the primitive level (L1): laser weeders work in 15 countries according to their manufacturer, which reports more than 200 growers across its laserweeding and tractor-autonomy products (Carbon Robotics, 2026), but each machine performs one job. An Embodied S2 could let one platform scout field, decide where weeding or harvesting is Envisioning Agentic Robotics: New Era of Robotic Systems needed, and switch between these jobs as conditions change. In mobility, robotaxis provide hundreds of thousands of paid rides per week in restricted operating domains (Korosec, 2026). Cars and drones are physical agents as well, and the same S2S1S0 organization applies to them. Their history also suggests how agentic robotics is likely to scale: domain by domain, with each operating domain widened only as evidence of safety accumulates. Common Patterns. Across these domains, evidence of unaided work in unstructured settings is strongest at L2. Some demonstrations extend toward workflows, but their reports do not yet establish all the conditions needed for reliable L3 claim. Longer operation has been reported only in structured or restricted domains, and wherever the fallback is disclosed, it is person. The same three changes recur: work assigned by instruction rather than by engineering or new data, supervision by exception rather than one operator per robot, and responsibility extended from single tasks to workflows and roles. Each change would widen the range of work for which deploying robot is worthwhile. The research directions in Section 6.2 address what delivering these changes would take. C.
